newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FORECAST - Signs of life in Australia jobs mkt.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Signs of life in Australia jobs mkt.

text.p: Australia's struggling labour market appears to be showing some tentative signs of life, although economists see it as still lacking the strength to make significant inroads into the unemployment rate.
This Thursday's jobs data is forecast to show a fourth consecutive rise in January, and forward indicators of the labour market are showing that some growth can be expected through 1997.
However, the early part of 1997 is still seen as soft for employment growth, and unemployment is expected to remain above 8.0 percent at least until the latter part of the year.

The median forecast of the 28 economists surveyed by Reuters last Friday was for jobs growth of 10,000 during January. That growth will not be enough to make any dent on the 8.6 percent unemployment rate.
Forecasts for employment range from a fall of 5,000 to a rise of 17,000, with economists seeing the risks to the downside after the strength of the December quarter.
Unemployment rate forecasts range from 8.4 to 8.8 percent.
Employment rose by a meagre 66,200 in 1996, with 54,500 of that coming in the December quarter. In the last nine months of the year, employment levels only fell once, in September.
"Job creation was not something for which 1996 will be remembered," said economist Akis Haralabopoulos at insurer and funds manager GIO Australia.
The tepid growth that did occur was unable to make any inroads into the unemployment rate, leaving it stuck around 8.5 percent for the past 18 months.

However, there are some preliminary signs that the worst may have passed for the labour market, with most of the weakness concentrated in the first half of 1996 and forward indicators suggesting that labour demand may have been picking up into 1997.
The ANZ job ad series for Janaury ahowed a 3.3 percent rise, the second rise in three months, and the largest for one year. The trend series was positive for the first time in two years.
ANZ chief economist Saul Eslake said the series was volatile over the summer period, but added "it does appear that the two year decline in the demand for labour may be coming to an end".
Other indicators, such as the Australian Bureau of Statistics' (ABS) job vacancy series, were also pointing to stronger growth.

The impact of the three interest rate cuts in the second half of 1996 should also begin having a positive impact. "A combination of low interest rates, relatively high company profitability, and a healthy medium term outlook for profits should be conducive to employment gains," GIO's Haralabopoulos said.

As well, the concession by the ABS last month that a new survey method had been understating employment growth by about 6,000 to 9,000 a month since August meant that the labour market had been stronger than reported.
"The ABS change in survey technique has effectively masked an improvement in labour market," Bankers Trust Australia senior economist David Bassanese said.
However, that did not mean the labour market was on the cusp of a cyclical improvement, he said, as the strength of the second half of 1996 could be a correction to a very weak first half.
